newsitem.title: INDIA: Indian steel sector seen unattractive till mid-97.
newsitem.headline: Indian steel sector seen unattractive till mid-97.

text.p: Securities firm Paribas Capital Markets said Indian steel stocks were not attractive in the medium term.

"At this point in the cycle the Indian steel sector is not attractive, by mid-1997 the worst may be over and it may deserve further consideration," Paribas analyst Rajeev Das said in a report on Indian steel industry on Friday.
Indian steel shares have underperformed not only the Indian market but also the Asian steel sector, Paribas said.

"The relentless addition of capacity in India continues," the report said. "In the last year several new plants have been announced suggesting an annual growth in steel supply of 12 percent while demand is only growing at 7.0 percent," it said.
Paribas said it expected supply to outstrip demand by 1997-98, requiring India to be a net exporter of steel.

Steel stocks in net exporting countries tend to sell at a discount to their markets due to their exposure to the global steel cycles and therefore India's status as a net exporter could have an adverse effect, the report said.
"We consider the market is partly discounting this."

With potential excess supply in certain products, steel prices should remain weak in India, it said. Although prices in the U.S. show some signs of firming up, Asian prices, especially those in Korea and Taiwan, still remain weak, it said.
"Apart from these industry related problems, some companies face specific problems and their valuation is going to depend more on investor sentiment than fundamentals," it said.

These factors, which have more to do with the management of these companies rather than the industry itself, have contributed to the decline in the valuation of the steel sector compared to rest of the market, Paribas said.
Paribas expected a slight fall in GDP growth and industrial production in 1996/97 to be followed by a recovery in 1997-98.
"We consider the industry may have to face rationalisation over the next couple of years and investment now requires identifying companies that should survive this," it said.
"On this basis, we believe SAIL and TISCO merit consideration," it said.
